analysis.one_liner: Cuts the top tax rate on investment gains and adjusts asset values for inflation.
analysis.headline: Introduced on the first day of the 107th Congress with 21 cosponsors, but the Ways and Means Committee never took it up and it expired without a vote in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would cut the top tax rate on capital gains from 20% to 15% for individuals and set a 28% rate for corporations, and it would let individuals adjust the purchase price of stocks and other assets upward to match inflation, so only gains above inflation would be taxed [S2] [S3]. Capital gains taxes are owed almost entirely by households that own stocks, businesses, and investment real estate, and that ownership is concentrated at the top of the income scale. The bill never got a committee markup or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Households with large investment portfolios, and corporations with capital gains, gain the most: the rate cut lowers their tax bill on every sale of stock, business assets, or property, and inflation indexing would erase tax on the part of a gain that just kept up with prices [S2] [S3]. People in the 15% bracket would pay a reduced 7.5% rate on gains, a smaller group [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Sets a maximum 15% capital gains rate for individuals, down from the then-current 20% top rate, and applies it even under the alternative minimum tax [S3].
Sets a 28% maximum capital gains rate for corporations in place of the standard corporate rates, which could run as high as 35% [S3].
Lets individuals add inflation to the cost basis of stock and tangible business property held more than three years, so only real gains above inflation are taxed [S3].
Taxes gains below the 15% income-tax bracket at 7.5%, and extends indexing through mutual funds, REITs, partnerships, and S corporations to their individual investors [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury would collect less revenue, which over time must be made up by other taxpayers through borrowing or by reducing spending. The tax savings would flow overwhelmingly to households at the top of the income distribution, because that is where taxable capital gains are concentrated.

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals the existing exclusion for gain on certain qualified small business stock, raising taxes for investors who sell shares of qualifying small companies [S3].
It caps the deduction of capital losses for individuals at the amount of their capital gains, which removes an existing benefit for taxpayers whose investments lost money [S3].
The inflation indexing adjustment applies only to individuals, not to corporations, and only to assets held more than three years, limiting who can use it and adding tax-calculation complexity [S3].

Cutting the rate on investment income reduces federal revenue; an honest supporter would have had to identify offsetting spending cuts, other taxes, or larger deficits, none of which this bill addresses [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the households and corporations that hold most capital assets, the bill is a straightforward tax cut. The offsetting costs land broadly: less federal revenue from everyone's taxes, plus the loss of the small business stock exclusion and the capital loss deduction that help other kinds of taxpayers. Because the benefit is concentrated at the top while the cost is spread across all taxpayers, the bill weighs clearly in favor of concentrated wealth.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never scheduled a markup or vote, and the bill expired when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Representative David Dreier introduced the bill on January 3, 2001, the opening day of the 107th Congress, making capital gains tax cuts one of the first bills filed by the new majority [S1] [S5].
The House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee the same day [S5].
The bill attracted 21 cosponsors, 18 Republicans and 3 Democrats [S4].
No further action was ever recorded; the committee took no markup or vote, and the bill died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the Treasury kept the revenue it would have forgone, and the House Ways and Means Committee's tax-writing agenda went to other bills instead. Wealthy investors and corporations got nothing from this bill, though they gained nothing to offset either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: General taxpayers; investors gained nothing here

for.name: Rep. David Dreier
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the first day of the 107th Congress and recruited cosponsors.

for.name: 3 of 208 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsors Reps. Karen McCarthy and Peter Deutsch.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the referral; never scheduled a markup or vote, letting the bill expire.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was heavily Republican: 18 of the 21 cosponsors were Republicans, and only 3 of the chamber's 208 Democrats signed on [S4].

industries.note: The rate cut and inflation indexing directly lower the tax bill on stock, business, and property sales, and taxable capital gains are concentrated among the wealthiest households. The revenue given up must be recovered from taxpayers generally.
A new 28% maximum rate on corporate capital gains replaces rates that could reach 35%, a direct cut for companies selling assets. Its cost is spread across all taxpayers.

The bill routes indexing benefits through regulated investment companies and real estate investment trusts to their shareholders, a benefit for fund investors, including many middle-income retirement savers. The gains remain concentrated among those who own fund shares.

The bill repeals the exclusion for gain on qualified small business stock, so investors selling qualifying small company shares would pay tax they currently avoid. This is a cost the bill imposes to help pay for the broader rate cut.
